title: Middleware: agent, chat and function
summary: Three interception points: around a whole agent run, around each model call and around each tool call. Each can inspect, change, short-circuit or replace the result.
useIf: You need a guardrail, audit log, allow-list, rate limit or result rewrite that must apply no matter what the model decides.
avoidIf: The rule belongs in the prompt, in tool code or in a context provider that merely adds information.

explain.md: Middleware forms a chain. Each link receives a context and a `next` callback. In Python the callback takes no argument: you mutate the shared context and `await call_next()`. In .NET each kind is a function callback and you call the supplied `next` [[tr4]]. Each kind can be function-based or class-based in Python (`AgentMiddleware`, `FunctionMiddleware`, `ChatMiddleware` with a `process` method), or declared with the `@agent_middleware`, `@function_middleware` and `@chat_middleware` decorators.

head: Kind
Context (Python)
Runs
Typical use
rows: `AgentContext`: agent, messages, session, options, stream, metadata, result
Allow-lists, argument validation, timing, ending the tool loop (.NET `Terminate`)

explain.md: **Order.** Agent-level middleware wraps run-level middleware. With agent middleware [A1, A2] and run middleware [R1, R2] the order is A1, A2, R1, R2, agent, R2, R1, A2, A1 [[tr4]]. **Termination.** In Python set `context.result` and raise `MiddlewareTermination`; in .NET set `FunctionInvocationContext.Terminate` to end the tool loop. Ending the loop can leave history with a function call that has no result, which may make it unusable for the next run [[tr4]].

blocks.title: Run and function middleware
Blocking and function middleware
blocks.code:
from agent_framework import (AgentContext, AgentResponse, Message,
    MiddlewareTermination, FunctionInvocationContext)

async def block_words(context: AgentContext, call_next):
    last = context.messages[-1] if context.messages else None
    if last and last.text and 'blocked' in last.text.lower():
        context.result = AgentResponse(
            messages=[Message(role='assistant', contents=['Blocked.'])])
        raise MiddlewareTermination(result=context.result)
    await call_next()

async def time_tool(context: FunctionInvocationContext, call_next):
    await call_next()
    print(context.function.name, 'done')

agent = Agent(client=client, middleware=[block_words, time_tool])
# run-level, this call only:
await agent.run('hi', middleware=[extra_logging])

explain.title: Streaming needs its own handler in .NET
explain.md: If you pass only `runFunc`, streaming calls run in non-streaming mode. The `Use(sharedFunc)` overload keeps streaming but cannot override the output [[tr4]].

whereToUse: Input guardrails: block or rewrite a user message before the model sees it
Tool governance: allow-list tool names, validate arguments, cap spend per tool
Audit: write who called what with which arguments to a compliance log
Result shaping: redact fields from the answer, or replace it, for both streaming and non-streaming runs
Rate limiting and early termination for abusive sessions

use: The rule must hold whatever the model decides: enforce it in code
You need to observe or change the call at one specific layer
You want to reuse one policy across many agents by registering it once
avoid: The need is only extra context or memory: a context provider is the right tool
The check is already inside one tool: validate there instead
You need a fail-closed control plane with verdicts across all layers: look at Agent Hooks (Python, experimental) [[tr46]]
flips: Policy must apply to remote agents too: register at the agent layer, since chat and function layers belong to the local pipeline
Streaming output must be checked before release: ordinary middleware cannot buffer it; Agent Hooks buffer streaming until output passes (Python, experimental)

pitfalls.symptom: A streaming client bypasses the guardrail
pitfalls.cause: .NET middleware registered with `runFunc` only, or the result override handles only `AgentResponse`
pitfalls.fix: Supply both handlers; in Python branch on `context.stream` and replace the generator for streaming

pitfalls.symptom: Next run fails after a tool was denied
pitfalls.cause: `Terminate` left a function call without a result in history
pitfalls.fix: Return a function result for every call or discard that history; test the resume path

pitfalls.symptom: Order surprises: run middleware fires inside agent middleware
pitfalls.fix: Draw the A1, A2, R1, R2 order before relying on side effects

scenarios.title: Allow-list tools for a customer-facing bot
scenarios.situation: A public chatbot has 12 tools registered, but only 4 are safe for anonymous users. Tool choice is the model's. A prompt injection could ask for a privileged tool.
constraints: Privileged tools exist in the same agent
Latency overhead must be under a few milliseconds
unknowns: Can the tool list be built per request instead?
Is the decision based on the user's role?
What should the model be told when a call is denied?
scenarios.question: How do you enforce the allow-list?

options.name: Do not register the privileged tools for this agent, and add function middleware as a second line of defence
options.why: A tool that is not registered cannot be called. The middleware catches mistakes in wiring.
options.tradeoff: Two agents or a per-request tool set to maintain.

options.name: Function middleware only, denying by name
options.tradeoff: The model still sees the tool schemas and may keep trying; one wiring bug exposes the tool.

options.name: A system prompt that says never call admin tools
options.why: Prompt text is not enforcement and injection can override it.
options.tradeoff: Fine as an extra hint, never as the control.

flips.if: Roles are many and change per request
flips.then: Build the tool list per request from a context provider with `extend_tools`, and keep the middleware check.

flips.if: Denials should be audited with the user id
flips.then: Log from the middleware using the session.

scenarios.takeaway: Remove what must not be called, and enforce the rest in code.

scenarios.title: Rewrite answers for a regulated channel
scenarios.situation: Answers must never contain an internal case id. The assistant streams tokens to a web client and also serves a non-streaming batch API.
constraints: Case ids follow a fixed pattern
Auditors want proof it cannot leak
unknowns: Can a partial id appear across stream chunks?
Is blocking acceptable or must the text be edited?
scenarios.question: What do you build?

options.name: Agent middleware that handles both result types (`AgentResponse` and a stream generator), with a buffer for chunk boundaries
options.why: It sits at the output boundary and covers both paths.
options.tradeoff: Buffering adds latency to the first streamed tokens.

options.name: Non-streaming middleware only
options.why: Streaming would bypass it, or in .NET fall back to non-streaming mode.
options.tradeoff: Right when the channel is batch-only.

options.name: Prompt the model not to print case ids
options.why: No guarantee and no proof for auditors.
options.tradeoff: Works as defence in depth only.

flips.if: Streaming must be held until a verdict arrives
flips.then: Evaluate Agent Hooks (Python, experimental), which buffer streaming until output passes.

flips.if: Only a few fixed phrases must be removed and the channel is batch-only
flips.then: Non-streaming middleware with a simple pattern replace is enough.

scenarios.takeaway: Test the streaming and non-streaming paths separately, because they are different code paths.

quiz.q: A Python agent has agent middleware [A1, A2] and run middleware [R1, R2]. In the whole execution, how many middleware steps run before the agent itself starts?
quiz.explain: Order is A1, A2, R1, R2, agent, R2, R1, A2, A1. Four steps come before the agent.

quiz.q: A .NET team registers `.Use(runFunc: Guard)` and finds streaming users skip their check. What is the most likely cause?
options: No `runStreamingFunc` was supplied, so streaming does not go through the guard as intended
Agent middleware never runs for streaming
quiz.explain: The docs say to provide both handlers. With only the non-streaming handler, streaming runs in non-streaming mode to satisfy it, and a shared overload cannot override output.

flashcards.front: How do you stop a Python run from middleware?
flashcards.back: Set `context.result`, then raise `MiddlewareTermination(result=...)`. This works for agent, function and chat middleware.

flashcards.front: What risk does ending the .NET tool loop with `Terminate` carry?
flashcards.back: History can keep a function call with no function result, which can make it unusable for later runs.

flashcards.front: Which middleware kind sees each tool call?
flashcards.back: Function-calling middleware (`FunctionInvocationContext`). Chat middleware sees each model call, agent middleware each run.
